title: Transactions & ACID
summary: A transaction is all-or-nothing. ACID is the four-property contract that makes it safe.

blocks.markdown:
A **transaction** is a sequence of database operations treated as one unit — either all succeed or none do.

- Banks move money in transactions so no partial state is ever visible.
- **ACID** is the four-property contract a database must honour for safe transactions.
- Properties: **Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability**.
- Without ACID, concurrent writes and crashes corrupt data.

A **transaction** groups one or more read/write operations into an all-or-nothing unit of work.

- **All steps commit** together, or **none** of them take effect.
- Example: transferring $200 — debit account A and credit account B must both happen, or neither does.
- A transaction starts implicitly or with `BEGIN` and ends with `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.

blocks.subTitle: BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK
Atomicity
blocks.markdown:
**Atomicity** — a transaction is indivisible: every operation inside it either all commits or all rolls back.

- *Why it matters:* without it a crash mid-transfer leaves one account debited and the other untouched.
- The DB writes a **log** (undo log) so it can reverse partial work on failure.
- "All or nothing" is the simplest mental model.

blocks.subTitle: Consistency
blocks.markdown:
**Consistency** — a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another; no constraint may be violated.

- *Why it matters:* it ensures business rules hold (total money in the system doesn't change after a transfer).
- The DB checks **integrity constraints** (foreign keys, NOT NULL, CHECK) before committing.
- If any rule breaks, the transaction is rejected.

blocks.subTitle: Isolation
blocks.markdown:
**Isolation** — concurrent transactions must not see each other's uncommitted changes; they behave as if they ran serially.

- *Why it matters:* without it, two simultaneous withdrawals can both read the same balance and both succeed, overdrawing the account.
- The DB uses locks or **MVCC** (multi-version concurrency control) to achieve this.
- Levels of isolation trade correctness for speed. See [isolation-levels](isolation-levels).

blocks.subTitle: Durability
blocks.markdown:
**Durability** — once a transaction commits, its changes survive any subsequent crash.

- *Why it matters:* a confirmed payment that vanishes after a server reboot is unacceptable.
- Achieved by flushing changes to a **write-ahead log (WAL)** on disk before acknowledging the commit.
- Durability is the property that makes `COMMIT` a promise.

blocks.subTitle: Quick reference
blocks.markdown:
One-line each:

| Property | Guarantee |
|---|---|
| Atomicity | All or nothing |
| Consistency | Only valid states |
| Isolation | No dirty reads between concurrent txns |
| Durability | Committed data survives crashes |

A transaction moves through well-defined states.

<<< Image: a clean state-diagram on a white background. Nodes (rounded rectangles, blue border): Active, Partially Committed, Committed, Failed, Aborted. Arrows: Active -> Partially Committed (labelled 'last op done'); Partially Committed -> Committed (labelled 'write to disk'); Active -> Failed (labelled 'error / crash'); Partially Committed -> Failed (labelled 'disk write fails'); Failed -> Aborted (labelled 'rollback complete'). Arrows are thin, dark grey. Minimal text, generous whitespace. >>>

- **Active** — operations executing.
- **Partially committed** — final operation done, not yet on disk.
- **Committed** — durable; visible to others.
- **Failed** → **Aborted** — rolled back; state as if it never ran.

The two ways a transaction ends:

- **COMMIT** — finalises all changes permanently; visible to other transactions; cannot be undone.
- **ROLLBACK** — discards every change in the transaction; DB returns to the state before `BEGIN`.

A failed transaction is always rolled back — by the application explicitly or by the DB on crash recovery. See [recovery-systems](recovery-systems).

Without transactions, two things go wrong:

- **Crashes** leave data half-written — one account debited, the other not credited.
- **Concurrency** lets two users read the same stale balance and both withdraw, creating phantom money.

Transactions give a clean, predictable contract: the outside world sees only committed states. Anything in between stays invisible.

Common mistakes:

- **Long-running transactions** hold locks too long, blocking other readers/writers.
- **Assuming ACID everywhere.** Many NoSQL databases don't offer full ACID — know your DB's guarantees.
- **Ignoring isolation level.** Default level isn't always serializable; dirty/phantom reads can still happen. See [isolation-levels](isolation-levels).
- **Catching exceptions and not rolling back.** A caught error without `ROLLBACK` leaves the transaction open.

blocks.subTitle: Explain ACID
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain ACID properties.**

**Atomicity** — all-or-nothing; partial writes never persist. **Consistency** — only valid states; constraints enforced. **Isolation** — concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work. **Durability** — committed data survives crashes via disk logs.

Anchor with an example: a bank transfer needs all four or money appears/disappears.

blocks.subTitle: Atomicity guarantee
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What does Atomicity guarantee?**

That no observer ever sees a transaction half-done. If any operation in the transaction fails, the database undoes all preceding operations in that transaction and returns to the state before `BEGIN`.

blocks.subTitle: Consistency vs Isolation
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Difference between Consistency and Isolation?**

**Consistency** is about the database's own rules (constraints, foreign keys) — the data must always be logically valid. **Isolation** is about transactions not interfering with each other while running concurrently.

Consistency asks "is the data valid?"; Isolation asks "can two transactions see each other?"
